extracted.intended_audience: readers of The New York Tribune; general educated public, commentators, and lawmakers interested in marriage/divorce law and moral debate
extracted.subtask_description: A public 1860 newspaper exchange debating legal, religious, moral, and lexical standards for marriage and divorce — contrasting single-cause (adultery/fornication) statutes with multi-cause statutes and differing conceptions of marriage's purpose. Contains philological, jurisprudential, and social arguments relevant to drafting/interpreting divorce law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage as a union for life
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage is, according to every standard dictionary and Christian teaching cited, 'a union for life, indissoluble at the pleasure of those married, or either of them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley argues one should not use the word 'marriage' for any other sort of union; to do so misleads the public and weakens social/moral restraints. He links the definition to social stability and the historic consensus of the Christian Church and lexicographers. If an arrangement permits separation at pleasure it should be given a different name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divorce valid only for fornication/adultery (single-cause rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jesus' teaching: 'Whosoever shall put away his wife, except it be for fornication, and shall marry another, committeth adultery' — i.e., adultery (fornication) is the only valid cause for divorce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as the Christian doctrinal standard and historical rebuttal to broader Mosaic permissions; used to justify single-cause statutes (as in New York) and to argue against liberalizing divorce grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divorce law may legitimately admit several causes (multi-cause rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The law should admit several causes for divorce (as in Indiana or Connecticut); a single-cause restriction is not necessarily conducive to public morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen contends humane laws permitting multiple causes alleviate domestic misery, prevent household vice, and allow correction of relationships that 'frustrate the holiest purposes' of marriage. He views such statutes as practical, preventive, and responsive to social realities rather than moral laxity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philological interpretation of 'ervah' / 'uncleanness' in divorce text
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hebrew word 'ervah' (translated 'nakedness' or 'uncleanness') should be read as a 'blemish' or 'something which displeases him' (not invariably 'adultery'), per authorities like Gesenius, Luther, and Ewald.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lexical and historical scholarship to interpret scriptural divorce texts; when other defining words are absent the term does not necessarily mean adultery. This affects whether Mosaic law was limited to adultery as the only ground for divorce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish immutable principles from adaptable legal details
rubrics_metrics.description: Great moral principles endure (e.g., 'Love is the fulfilling of the law'), but the details of civil laws may change as the world changes; a law adapted to one age may cease to be suitable in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen argues jurisprudence should allow reform of legal particulars without abandoning eternal moral principles; Jesus' acceptance/rejection of Mosaic permissions is invoked as precedent for discarding details rendered unsuitable by social change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess divorce by whether marriage's higher purposes are frustrated
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage has higher ends (beyond mere reproduction) — love, mutual moral development, care — and 'whatever violates these defeats the Divine end of Marriage, and supplies rightful cause' for dissolving the relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen frames a moral criterion: if the relationship defeats the institution's true intent (household strife, domestic hatred, inhuman treatment), termination may be not only permissible but morally required for the good of virtue and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology integrity: reserve 'marriage' for indissoluble unions
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'marriage' denotes a lifelong covenant; applying it to temporary or easily-dissolved unions is a misuse of language and conceals an important moral difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley insists on lexical precision to preserve social meaning and moral expectations; he suggests inventing a distinctive name for unions that allow termination before death, warning that appropriation of 'marriage' would blur moral and legal boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawgiver must account for human fallibility and attainable demands
rubrics_metrics.description: A law that demands impossibilities (e.g., that all persons always choose perfectly) will fail; statutes should consider the powers likely at people's disposal and be attainable in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen argues laws should be humane and realistic: because mature foresight is rare and honest mistakes occur, legal remedies (including divorce for multiple causes) are warranted to correct irreversible social harms and relieve victims of immoral situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-order/societal interest in discouraging easy divorce
rubrics_metrics.description: Making divorce easy invites sensuality and selfishness; indissolubility is a social restraint limiting libertinism and protecting society's moral fabric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley warns that liberal divorce regimes risk promoting ephemeral unions and repeated remarriage, with historical examples (Roman liberty of divorce) used to argue for restrictive laws to prevent social decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children's welfare as a decisive metric
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging the validity or honorability of a sexual union ask: 'Would they gladly have children born of it? Would they proudly acknowledge those children...and fulfil toward them all duties of parents?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley uses this test to assess whether a union is true and honorable; unions that are intended to be childless or where parentage would be disavowed are viewed as improper and not genuinely marital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil law supremacy and legal recognition irrespective of religious opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: State codes (e.g., Connecticut, Indiana) declare what constitutes a legal marriage/divorce; civil law is supreme in the country and remains in force until legally repealed — religious opposition does not nullify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen emphasizes that legislative enactments determine legal status and that debates invoking religious doctrine do not override enacted statutes; practitioners and citizens must respect the law as the operative standard for civil rights and statuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret scripture contextually — concessions vs. permanent law
rubrics_metrics.description: Jesus' remark that 'Moses, for the hardness of your hearts, suffered you to put away your wives' is evidence that some Mosaic permissions were concessions to social conditions, not eternal prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deriving civil law from scripture, interpret passages in historical/contextual light; some biblical permissions may be situational and not binding as permanent civil rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid moralizing motive-judgment when assessing law reformers' intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: When legislators or citizens favor more-reasonable divorce laws they may act from conscientious motives (attempting to reduce suffering), not merely egotism or moral decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owen rebukes presumptive attribution of selfish motives to reformers and reminds that only the divine can read hearts; legal evaluation should consider sincere humanitarian intent as a legitimate basis for reform.
